SP Flash Tool: Unmodified Firmware Utility for Windows

 

 💻 PowerShell Installer

 

 

 

---

SP Flash Tool is a command-line utility for flashing firmware images to supported MediaTek-based devices from a Windows x64 host. It handles scatter-file parsing, download-agent handoff, and partition-level write operations through a single scriptable interface. The tool targets technicians and developers working in offline or air-gapped environments; it does not perform device unlocking, bypass security controls, or modify firmware beyond what the provided image files specify. Scope is limited to the flashing workflow described here, and behavior against unsupported chipsets or malformed scatter files is not guaranteed.

 ✅ Requirements

- OS: Windows 10 / 11
- Shell: PowerShell 5.1+ or PowerShell 7+
- Network: internet access to download the script
- Privileges: standard user

 Features

Operates as a single-binary CLI with no runtime dependencies beyond the host OS; all functionality is exposed through subcommands and flags documented in the Usage and Flags sections.
- Accepts device configuration and flash-operation descriptors from local files; the tool reads and writes only paths you specify and performs no network calls during execution.
- Reports deterministic exit codes for every terminal condition, allowing reliable scripting and CI integration; the full mapping is defined in the Exit codes section.
- Emits structured, line-oriented output suitable for log capture and parsing, with verbosity controlled by explicit flags rather than environment inference.
- Supports batch execution of sequential operations defined in a single descriptor file, stopping or continuing on error according to a declared policy.
- Scope is limited to the operations enumerated in the Flags reference; device-specific protocols, vendor signing, and firmware validation are outside the current implementation and are not implied by any flag.
- Validates descriptor syntax before any device interaction and fails fast with a diagnostic identifying the offending line and field.
- Performs no privilege escalation and requires the caller to supply whatever access the target interface demands; permission failures are surfaced verbatim rather than retried silently.
- Cross-platform builds share the same argument grammar and exit-code contract, though hardware access paths differ by OS and are documented per platform in the Recipes section.
- All processing occurs locally against user-provided inputs; no telemetry, remote logging, or configuration upload is performed.

 Usage

Invoke the tool from a terminal with the target device descriptor and, optionally, a flash plan file. At minimum, a single argument identifying the connected device or a plan is required; the tool enumerates attached hardware and refuses to proceed if more than one candidate matches without an explicit selector.

 

By default the tool performs a read-only inventory of the device, prints the detected chipset and partition map, and exits without writing. Writing is opt-in and must be requested with the appropriate operation flag. Dry-run output is identical to a real run except that no data is committed.

Operational scope is limited to devices the tool can enumerate over the supported transport. It does not manage firmware for arbitrary hardware and will report an unsupported target rather than attempt a generic write. If a device is not recognized, the tool exits non-zero and produces no partial state.

Configuration precedence, from highest to lowest: command-line arguments, the plan file, the profile config in the working directory, and built-in defaults. Values resolved from a lower-priority source are overridden silently unless -verbose is set, in which case each resolution is logged to stderr.

Standard streams behave predictably: progress and human-readable status go to stderr, machine-readable output goes to stdout. This allows piping stdout to a file or another process without progress noise. Exit status follows the codes documented in the Exit codes section; callers should branch on the code rather than parsing messages.

For repeatable workflows, capture an explicit plan with -plan-out and re-run it later with -plan . Plans are plain text and can be reviewed and edited before execution. The tool never reads a plan from an implicit location and never executes one found next to the binary.

Advanced operation overrides are available under the -modifier namespace for device-specific tuning. These are documented individually under Flags and are intended for cases where defaults do not match a particular hardware revision. They are not required for standard use and can produce inconsistent results if applied without understanding the target's expected sequence; the tool will not prevent you from using them, but it logs a notice when one is set.

 Flags

 -p , -port — Binds the local service to the specified TCP port. Defaults to 8080 . Values outside 1–65535 are rejected at startup.

- -d , -device — Selects the target device by identifier. Only the first matching device is used; if none matches, the process exits with a non-zero status.

- -o , -output — Writes results to the given file path instead of standard output. Parent directories must already exist; they are not created implicitly.

- -dry-run — Performs validation and resolves all inputs without transmitting data or modifying any device state. Useful for verifying configuration before a real run.

- -verbose — Emits extended diagnostic logging to standard error. Log volume is significantly higher and may impact timing on slow terminals.

- -timeout — Sets the per-operation timeout. Defaults to 30 . A value of 0 disables the timeout entirely; this is not recommended for unattended runs.

- -no-color — Disables ANSI color sequences in output. Applied automatically when output is not attached to a TTY.

- -v , -version — Prints the version string and exits. No other flags are processe
